summary: No critical or high findings. A line-level sweep of the Codex tree (secrets shapes, shell/SQL/path construction, crypto and randomness, unsafe blocks, extractors, dynamic execution in the TS/Python layers) comes back clean at the pattern level: the only credential-shaped literals in production code are intentional published identifiers (Statsig client key, Sentry DSN, OAuth public client id) already judged by the observability and security-design scans; every other hit is a test fixture under #[cfg(test)]. First-party command execution is argv-based throughout - the only string-to-shell sinks are the model's own commands (the product's purpose, gated by the approval+sandbox design) and static updater constants. SQL is uniformly parameterized, SHA-1 appears only in cache-key/git-blob-id roles, OAuth PKCE and state come from a CSPRNG, websocket bearer tokens are compared in constant time, and zero TLS-verification overrides exist anywhere in the tree. The two attention items are hygiene-grade: ~818 unsafe blocks across 141 files (concentrated in the sandbox/FFI crates where they belong) carry only ~89 SAFETY-style comments and no lint enforcement, and the curated-plugins zip extractor lacks the decompressed-size cap and mode sanitization that the sibling tar extractor has.

findings.title: Embedded identifiers are intentional publishables: Statsig client key, Sentry DSN, OAuth public client id
findings.description: Three credential-shaped constants ship in the source, and all three are identifiers designed to be embedded in clients rather than secrets: the Statsig client API key used for the default metrics exporter (already judged by observability-scan as a low-severity default-destination issue, with a recommendation to treat it as rotatable config), the Sentry DSN used only for user-initiated feedback envelopes (DSNs are publishable by design), and the OAuth client id for the PKCE login flow (a public client - PKCE S256 exists precisely so no client secret is needed; an env var override CODEX_APP_SERVER_LOGIN_CLIENT_ID is provided). None grants access to user data by itself. Reported as inventory so future secret-scans do not re-flag them; the design-level judgments stand with the sibling scanners.

evidence.note: client-side Statsig key; posture judged by observability-scan
Sentry DSN - publishable ingest identifier, used only for consent-based feedback upload
OAuth public client id for the PKCE flow - no client secret exists

findings.title: Secrets hygiene clean: every credential-shaped hit outside the three publishables is a test fixture
findings.description: Sweeps for credential prefixes (sk-, ghp_, AKIA, xox, PEM private-key headers), api_key/secret/password assignments with long literal values, and long base64-like literals in config files produced ~35 candidates; every one was read in context and all are test fixtures: obviously-fake tokens in sanitizer and credential-broker tests, throwaway RSA keys inside #[cfg(test)] modules of the agent-identity and login crates, and 'bedrock-api-key-test'-style placeholders. The long literals in manifests are git revision pins, not tokens. Notably the test suite actively defends storage hygiene: one test re-executes itself under umask 000 to assert the OAuth token fallback file is still created 0600. No real credential material was found in the tree.

evidence.note: test module boundary - the PEM key below it is a fixture
throwaway RSA key used only to sign test JWTs
test asserting token file stays 0600 even under a permissive umask

findings.title: Shell/command construction clean: argv-based first-party calls; string-to-shell only for model commands and static constants
findings.description: All first-party process launches reviewed build argv arrays and pass them without a shell: git/gh helpers push fixed flags plus caller args as separate argv entries, hooks and MCP header commands run user-configured (not attacker-supplied) command vectors, and the self-updater's cmd.exe /C path receives only static strings from the UpdateAction enum ('npm install -g @openai/codex' etc.) - the code even routes the PowerShell installer around cmd.exe specifically to avoid metacharacter parsing. The only place arbitrary strings reach 'sh -lc' is derive_exec_args, which wraps the model's own proposed command - that is the product's purpose, and it is gated by the approval policy and OS sandbox layers documented by security-design-scan, so it is a design boundary, not an injection defect. No format!-built command strings from external data were found.

evidence.note: the one string-to-shell sink: the model's own command, approval+sandbox gated
updater commands are static constants, no interpolation
representative first-party pattern: argv vector, fixed flags, no shell

findings.title: SQL clean: all sqlx queries use bound parameters; no string-built SQL found
findings.description: The SQLite state layer (state crate, TUI log db, doctor thread inventory) issues queries exclusively through sqlx with '?' placeholders and .bind(), or as fixed DDL/PRAGMA strings. A sweep for format!-constructed SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE strings and query(&format!(...)) calls across all Rust crates returned zero real hits. SQL injection surface: none found.

evidence.snippet: sqlx::query("UPDATE threads SET updated_at_ms = ?, recency_at_ms = ? WHERE id = ?")
evidence.note: representative bound-parameter query in the state runtime

findings.title: SHA-1 confined to non-security roles: cache keys, git blob ids, telemetry identity hashes
findings.description: SHA-1 appears at ~12 call sites (connectors directory cache, MCP tool-catalog cache, image/audio caches via a shared sha1_digest helper, git blob object ids in the turn diff tracker, analytics id hashing). Every use is identity/cache-keying where collision resistance against a motivated attacker is not load-bearing, and the shared helper's doc comment explicitly frames it as a cache-key utility. Security-relevant hashing uses SHA-256 throughout: PKCE S256 challenges, hook trust hashes (sha256: prefix), bundled-bubblewrap binary verification, and websocket token digests. Fitness-for-purpose verdict: appropriate.

evidence.snippet: /// Useful for content-based cache keys when you want to avoid staleness
evidence.note: shared sha1_digest helper self-documents its cache-key role

evidence.snippet: /// Compute the Git SHA-1 blob object ID for the given content (bytes).
evidence.note: SHA-1 required here for git blob-id compatibility

findings.title: Websocket auth compares token digests in constant time; disabled JWT library checks are re-implemented manually
findings.description: The app-server transport's websocket auth is careful in two ways worth documenting. Capability-token mode hashes the presented bearer token with SHA-256 and compares against the expected digest with constant_time_eq_32, eliminating both timing oracles and accidental logging of raw tokens. Signed-bearer-token mode looks alarming at first read - validate_exp/validate_nbf/validate_aud are all set to false on the jsonwebtoken Validation - but this is a mitigated pattern, not a gap: decode only checks the HS256 signature, and validate_jwt_claims then enforces exp, nbf, iss and aud manually with an explicit max_clock_skew_seconds tolerance (exp is a required, non-optional claim in the deserialized struct). Grepped as a candidate finding, confirmed compensated after reading.

evidence.note: constant-time comparison of token digests
library check disabled - candidate finding
...but expiry is re-enforced manually with clock-skew handling

findings.title: Security-relevant randomness uses a CSPRNG; zero TLS-verification overrides in the tree
findings.description: The OAuth flow generates the PKCE code verifier (64 bytes) and the callback state token (32 bytes) with rand::rng() - rand 0.9's ThreadRng, a ChaCha-based CSPRNG seeded from OS entropy - which is adequate for both roles; the state token is single-use on a localhost callback, so its non-constant-time comparison offers no practical oracle. A sweep for TLS verification bypasses (danger_accept_invalid_certs, NoVerifier, rejectUnauthorized, NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED, verify=False) across Rust, TypeScript and Python found zero hits; HTTP uses reqwest over rustls per the workspace manifest. No home-rolled primitives were found - hashing, signatures (ed25519-dalek, jsonwebtoken) and TLS all come from standard crates.

evidence.note: PKCE verifier entropy: 64 bytes from ThreadRng (CSPRNG)
OAuth state token: 32 CSPRNG bytes

findings.title: ~818 unsafe blocks in 141 files, rightly concentrated in sandbox/FFI crates, but SAFETY comments are sparse and unenforced
findings.description: The workspace contains roughly 818 unsafe blocks plus 49 unsafe fns across 141 files, overwhelmingly in the places that genuinely need them: linux-sandbox (fork/exec, capget, inotify), windows-sandbox-rs (token/ACL/WFP Win32 FFI), the macOS outbound-proxy FFI, pty, and shell-escalation fd-passing. Hygiene is uneven: only ~89 SAFETY-style comments exist tree-wide, and sampled FFI-heavy files (http-client macos proxy: 37 unsafe/0 SAFETY; windows token.rs: 23/0; shell-escalation socket.rs: 18/0) argue invariants only occasionally via doc comments (e.g. 'The caller guarantees that every element of buf is initialized' on assume_init). The load-bearing linux sandbox entry does document its subtle blocks (the capget ABI comment) while leaving trivial libc wrappers bare - a defensible norm, but nothing enforces it: the workspace lint table has rust = {} (no unsafe_code forbid for pure-logic crates) and clippy::undocumented_unsafe_blocks is not enabled. Read samples showed no incorrect-looking unsafe; this is a documentation/enforcement gap, not an observed soundness defect, hence low.

evidence.note: no workspace-level unsafe_code lint; undocumented_unsafe_blocks absent from the clippy table below
load-bearing fd-passing helper; invariant stated in doc comment, no per-block SAFETY

evidence.snippet: // SAFETY: capability ABI version 3 uses a [version, pid] header and
evidence.note: the counter-example: subtle syscalls in the sandbox entry are documented

findings.recommendation: Enable clippy::undocumented_unsafe_blocks (at least for the sandbox, escalation and FFI crates) and add #![forbid(unsafe_code)] or the workspace rust lint to the many pure-logic crates that need no unsafe, so the census stays confined and every remaining block carries its argument.

findings.title: Dynamic code execution is confined to an embedded V8 built with its sandbox feature; no eval in the scripting layers
findings.description: The only dynamic code execution engine in the product is the 'code mode' runtime, which embeds V8 with the v8_enable_sandbox feature enabled - V8's internal heap sandbox, an appropriate hardening choice for running model-generated JavaScript in-process. In the TypeScript SDK and CLI wrapper there is no eval/new Function and process launching uses node:child_process spawn with argv arrays (no shell:true anywhere); the Python layer's only exec() calls are import-star assertions in tests. Verdict: the scripting layers are clean, and the one deliberate code-execution surface ships with its engine-level sandbox on.

evidence.note: V8 heap sandbox enabled for the code-mode runtime
TS SDK launches the binary via spawn argv, never a shell string

findings.title: Plugin bundle tar extractor is hardened: traversal rejected component-wise, links refused, total size capped
findings.description: The tar.gz unpacker for plugin bundles - a path where third-party archive content meets the local filesystem - implements the full defensive checklist: every entry path is rebuilt component-by-component with ParentDir, RootDir and Prefix components rejected outright (zip-slip/traversal), hard-link and symlink entries are refused entirely (closing the link-then-write escape), unsupported entry types error out, and a running decompressed-size total is enforced against a caller-supplied cap with checked arithmetic (decompression-bomb). The packing side mirrors this with a size-limited buffer. This is the strongest extractor implementation pattern available short of extracting into a sandboxed process.

evidence.note: traversal components rejected during component-wise path rebuild
link entries refused - blocks link-then-write escapes
decompressed-size cap with overflow-checked accounting

findings.title: Curated-plugins zip extractor lacks the size cap and mode sanitization its sibling tar extractor has
findings.description: extract_zipball_to_dir, which unpacks the curated-plugins zipball during startup sync, guards traversal correctly (zip's enclosed_name() plus a Normal-components-only rebuild) but, unlike the plugin tar extractor in the same crate, imposes no cap on total decompressed size (std::io::copy per entry with no accounting - a zip bomb inflates unchecked into CODEX_HOME) and applies the archive's unix permission bits verbatim via set_permissions, so archive-supplied modes (including setuid/setgid bits, inert for user-owned files but still undesirable) land on disk unfiltered. Exploitability is limited: the bytes come only from pinned first-party sources (api.github.com zipball of openai/plugins, or the chatgpt.com backend export) over HTTPS, so an attacker needs upstream or CA compromise - hence low, as an internal-consistency hardening gap rather than a reachable vulnerability.

evidence.note: traversal is guarded - this part is correct
uncapped per-entry copy: no decompressed-size accounting
archive-supplied unix mode applied without masking

findings.recommendation: Reuse the tar path's total-size enforcement for the zip extractor and mask applied modes to permission bits (mode & 0o777, or just preserve the executable bit), so both extractors offer the same guarantees regardless of source trust.

findings.title: Coverage: what this scan swept, and what it could not
findings.description: Swept and judged in this run: (1) secrets - credential prefixes, assignment shapes, PEM headers, and long base64-ish literals across Rust/TS/Python/config, ~35 candidates all read in context; (2) injection - shell invocation sites, format!-built commands, sqlx call sites, and the updater/git/hook launch paths, with representative input-to-sink traces; (3) crypto - hash-algorithm roles, RNG sources, TLS-override patterns, token comparison, JWT validation; (4) unsafe/native - a census of unsafe blocks with deep reads in the linux sandbox entry and shell-escalation fd-passing, plus SAFETY-comment density sampling of the four heaviest FFI files; (5) input handling - both archive extractors read line-by-line, dynamic execution in TS/Python swept; (6) the shell-escalation channel checked for external attack surface (none: it uses inherited socketpairs, not filesystem sockets). Not covered: dependency CVE status (no advisory database in this scan - the repo does run cargo-deny with an [advisories] table, so the mechanism exists); fuzzing or dynamic testing of parsers (tree-sitter shell parsing, protocol deserializers) - only their construction was reviewed; exhaustive TOCTOU analysis of check-then-use filesystem paths (the design scan documents the deliberate validate-but-still-sandbox stance that bounds this class); Windows FFI call-correctness in windows-sandbox-rs (counted and sampled, not audited call-by-call); and third_party/ plus vendored code, skipped per the Sokrates ignore rules with no local patches to vendored source observed in the sweeps.

evidence.note: dependency-advisory mechanism present (cargo-deny); CVE adjudication itself is out of this scan's scope
